top_choice_rationale: P001 (B005: Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) does best on the common test. Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices changed what can be credibly measured, namely substitution, market power and merger effects from market data. About three decades of use and critique are on record, so durability can be judged from evidence rather than predicted. The credit core is one jointly authored contribution, and the citation can be limited to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which avoids overclaiming for Berry and Levinsohn the dynamic-industry strand or the broader empirical-IO tradition (Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard, Levin). Its main weaknesses are that it is a methods prize without a single headline finding and that estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form. I judge these acceptable if the citation rewards the method and does not imply settled magnitudes. This is my own weighing of colleagues' statements, which I have not independently verified, and the number of supporters is not merit. P002 (B030: Autor, Hanson, Dorn) is second because its design-based evidence on labour-market adjustment is strong and its trio is clean, but the persistence, magnitude and shift-share debates make it less mature. I rank it above no award because it is a credible, well-attributed contribution. P000 is last because at least two proposals are, in my judgement, worthy of the prize.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for the credited names on P001 or P002. My profile shows institutional proximity to Tommy Andersson (Lund colleague, who also prefers B005) and to Jan Teorell (formerly at Lund), so agreement with them is not independent confirmation. My field is economic history, not industrial organisation, but my reasoning draws on an analogy with historical measurement, which a reader may weigh as a bias. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
